newsitem.title: CHINA: FEATURE - Chinese go for Hong Kong kitsch near handover.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Chinese go for Hong Kong kitsch near handover.

text.p: Communist China may be wary about sullying what it touts as its biggest event of 1997 with crass consumerism, but mainland businessmen are gaily creating kitsch to cash in on the return of Hong Kong to Beijing's rule.

Hong Kong watches, coins and refrigerator magnets are just some of the baubles that China's entrepreneurs have cooked up to tap into a wave of patriotic sentiment over Beijing's resumption of sovereignty over the territory at midnight on June 30.

"A lot of Chinese are buying these things because people are hoping that China will become more powerful after Hong Kong's return to the motherland," said Wang Wenbing, who runs a stall in Beijing selling commemorative Hong Kong watches.
Chinese media have given prominent coverage to the handover, with every television and radio newscast reminding the populace of the number of days left to the handover.
Each evening, China Central Television devotes a special minute before its primetime national news to a historical nugget on the British colony.
In Beijing's central Tiananmen Square a huge clock ticks off each remaining second.
GET YOUR COUNTDOWN WATCH

Wang's timepieces are a bit more ordinary. Most bear a beaming visage of late paramount leader Deng Xiaoping -- who negotiated Hong Kong's return from Britain in 1984 -- and the slogan: "97 Hong Kong Returns to the Motherland".
"My friends would sometimes give me these type of watches as presents, so I figured these watches would be hot sellers," said Wang, 31.
"Sales are pretty good," he said, adding that he had sold an average of two of the 97 yuan (US$12) watches a day for the last two months. Most buyers are Chinese collectors and foreigners.
Wang is not the only one cashing in on the handover.
China's young entrepreneurs, whose talents were unleashed by Deng's capitalist-inspired reforms, have dreamed up all sorts of goodies to appeal to the sentimental patriot.

Li Jun, the scruffy, bohemian vice-manager of Beijing's New Day Handicraft Co Ltd said his firm's hand-painted refrigerator magnets showing a suitcase-toting British bulldog boarding an airplane as a panda waves a Chinese flag are big winners.
"We've seen a lot of reports about Hong Kong's handover," Li says. "We are using a cartoon-like format to bring a sense of humour."
CULTURAL WATCHDOGS ON THE LOOKOUT
But China's cultural commissars are watching the likes of Wang and Li carefully, yanking from the marketplace any product deemed inappropriate.

"We have set restrictions on use of '1997', 'Hong Kong's return' and regional emblems on some products," said an official with the Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office, which takes its orders from China's State Council, or cabinet.
Only a handful of firms are authorised to produce the flag that Hong Kong will fly when it becomes a Special Administrative Region of China.
Factories hoping to capitalise on the handover must apply for approval with the office, the official said, adding that the government had issued official sets of stamps, coins and cards.
In late 1995, Beijing banned the use of "1997" in brand names after officials discovered that cigarette and alcohol producers were freely labelling their products to boost sales.
"(The restrictions) are to prevent over-commercialisation of Hong Kong's return in 1997," the official said. "The return is a serious matter."
NO JOKE TO HANDOVER ENFORCERS
China's marketing enforcers appear determined to guarantee the purity of the handover.

Police and industrial officials in the eastern province of Jiangsu recently seized more than one million yuan ($120,000) worth of ersatz commemorative Hong Kong handover badges, said a recent edition of the official People's Daily Overseas Edition.
"Other than the People's Bank of China, no unit or person is authorised to manufacture '97 Hong Kong Returns to the Motherland commemorative badges or coins, the newspaper said.

However, while Beijing has pumped up Hong Kong's return as the patriotic event of the year, if not the decade, many souvenir seekers have more material aims in mind as they rush to snap up such goods.

The price of one official silver commemorative coin issued last July to mark the handover had skyrocketed to 4,000 yuan from an initial 320 yuan, prompting authorities to warn of overheating on the coin market.
"Demand is really high for these items," said one office worker in Beijing. "But it's not necessarily so much out of patriotism as it is the search for a good investment."
